name: mapper
intent: Insert one object - the mapper - between two subsystems whose representations differ, so each side keeps its own model and every translation rule lives in a single place instead of leaking into both.
problem: Two subsystems must exchange data, but they speak different representations: DTO versus domain object, wire format versus in-memory model, vendor schema versus local types. If each side converts for itself, the translation is duplicated or scattered, both sides learn each other's internals, and every change to either representation ripples across the boundary. Changing one side is often impossible (external system, legacy code) or undesirable (the domain model must stay ignorant of transport and storage).
context: Boundary work where the two representations have different owners or evolve at different rates and at least one side must stay ignorant of the other: remote calls and API payloads, message endpoints, persistence seams, third-party SDKs, or format and schema versions during a migration. The characteristic signal is that the conversion carries real semantics - renamed fields, restructured shapes, units, defaults, absent-versus-null - rather than a cast or a renamed interface.
benefits: Neither side depends on the other: the domain keeps its own model and the transport, storage or vendor side keeps its schema, so either can be replaced or upgraded behind the mapper.
Translation exists once: field names, structure, units, defaults and absent-value policy live in one reviewable object instead of being re-improvised at every call site on both sides.
The boundary becomes testable: a mapper is a pure, dependency-light unit that can be table-tested against the awkward cases (missing fields, unknown values, defaults, units, time zones).
The two representations can evolve independently: adding a field on one side becomes a mapper change rather than a cross-cutting edit of both subsystems.
Information hiding: each side's internals stop at the mapper, which decides what crosses - useful for redaction, stable public shapes and keeping persistence or protocol types out of the domain.
It gives boundary policy a home: version negotiation, format selection and defaulting rules have one owner instead of being folklore at the call sites.
tradeoffs: An extra artefact layer to write and maintain: for a handful of identical fields the mapper costs more than the coupling it removes, and hand-written mapping code is repetitive by nature.
Silent drift: mapping is invisible to most type systems, so adding a field on one side leaves the mapper stale and the value missing with no compile error unless the mapping is generated or tested.
Mapping layers attract logic: validation, defaults, authorisation and business rules creep in until the mapper is a second, shadow implementation of the domain.
Copying costs: every crossing builds and copies intermediate objects, and a mapper that reaches into lazy objects (or triggers queries) becomes an N+1 problem on hot paths.

The invocation problem: neither representation should call the mapper directly, so a third party must - service layer, gateway, endpoint, interceptor or framework hook - and getting that trigger wrong or duplicating it is where mapper designs fail.
Three artefacts to keep in step (two representations plus the mapper); without generated mapping or contract tests, version skew between them surfaces only as bad production data.

participants.responsibility: The object graph, message payload or record on one side of the boundary, in the shape that side owns. It stays ignorant of the other representation and of the mapper.
The shape the other side expects - domain object, DTO, document or vendor type. It too stays ignorant of the mapper and of the source side's internals.

Owns every translation rule between the two representations: field names, structure, types, units, defaults, absent/null policy and what is deliberately dropped. Contains no I/O and no business rules.
Triggers the mapping at the right moment - service layer, gateway, endpoint, interceptor, ORM or framework hook - because neither representation may call the mapper itself.
Selects the mapper for a representation pair or version when several exist, so the choice is configured rather than hard-coded at the invoker.

Declarative description of the mapping (annotations, profiles, schema, serializer attributes) when the implementation is generated or configured rather than hand-written; it is the mapper's specification, not a second mapper.

use_cases: API and remote boundaries: convert domain objects to and from request/response DTOs so no transport type reaches the domain and no domain type leaks onto the wire.
Persistence seam (specialized as Data Mapper): load and store domain objects in relational rows, documents or key-value entries without the model knowing the schema or the store.
Messaging (specialized as Messaging Mapper): translate domain events and commands to and from message payloads plus headers, keeping both the domain and the message contract clean.
Third-party integration: map vendor SDK types, status codes, money, dates and units into local types at one controlled place instead of across the call sites.
Legacy coexistence and migration: translate between a fixed old schema and a new model (an anti-corruption layer is one way to host the mapper) while both run side by side.
Wire-format versions: convert between payload versions (for example v1 and v2 shapes) during a rolling upgrade, with the compatibility policy in one object.
Presentation: assemble view models or read models from domain aggregates, and map write commands back, keeping the presentation shape out of the domain.

ORM adoption in DDD bounded contexts: when introducing Hibernate (Java), Doctrine (PHP), Entity Framework Core (.NET) or SQLAlchemy (Python) into a rich domain model, a Data Mapper layer keeps the domain completely free of persistence infrastructure.
Event-sourced systems: serialize aggregate state to and from an event stream or projection, where the event schema is external and must not bleed into the domain model.
GraphQL resolvers: map domain entities to GraphQL response shapes and resolve input arguments back into domain commands, isolating the schema from the underlying model.
Compile-time Java bean mapping: MapStruct generates type-safe mapper implementations from annotated interfaces without reflection, keeping structural translation explicit and reviewable.
.NET object boundaries: AutoMapper profiles define convention-based object-to-object maps for projecting domain models into DTOs; complex semantic rules should remain explicit outside the profiles.
ORM persistence seams: SQLAlchemy's declarative mapping configures Python classes against tables and properties, providing a concrete Data Mapper realization at the storage boundary.
avoid_when: The two representations are the same or differ in a single field: an inline conversion at that one call site is simpler and honest.
You own both sides and can change one: align the representations, or refactor the interface (Adapter), instead of installing a permanent translation layer.
Only the callable surface differs, not the data: that is Adapter, and a single reusable value conversion is Converter, not a mapper layer.
The translation is really business logic (pricing, eligibility, invariants): it belongs in the domain or a domain service, not in the boundary mapper.
A framework already owns the mapping declaratively and adequately (serializer attributes, generated mappers, ORM mapping): declaring the fields beats writing a second mapper by hand.
anti_patterns: God mapper: one class or one layer that maps every pair of types in the system, branching per caller until it can neither be tested nor reviewed.
Leaky mapper: exposing the source object through the target (returning it, sharing mutable collections, leaking lazy proxies) so callers couple to the other side anyway.
Scattered conversion: the pattern inverted - every call site does its own field copying, so the two models are effectively coupled everywhere.
Reflection roulette: a generic convert-anything mapper that copies by name, silently drops what it cannot match and cannot state its own rules.
Mapper as domain logic: validation, defaults and business rules move into the mapper to avoid touching the model, leaving invariants outside the domain.
Round-trip amnesia: the mapper rebuilds objects field by field and loses identity, aggregate invariants or ownership, so load-then-save is not idempotent.
design_principles: Separation of concerns: representation translation is its own responsibility, separate from domain behaviour and from transport or persistence mechanics.
Single responsibility: one mapper per pair of representations, named for both sides.
Dependency inversion: each side depends only on its own model; the mapper lives in the outer layer and depends on both, so the core stays independent.
Information hiding: neither representation's internals cross the boundary - only what the mapper deliberately translates.
Open/closed: new representations and versions arrive as new mappers, so existing models stay closed for modification.
Explicit over implicit: mapping rules are written or declared where they can be reviewed and tested, never left to silent structural coercion.
best_practices: Give the mapping one home per pair (module, class, profile or instance set) and let nothing else copy fields across that boundary.
Write the mapping as data in, data out: no network, database or filesystem calls inside a mapper, so it stays a pure function of its input.
Decide per field and per direction how absent, unknown and added fields behave (fail, default, ignore, quarantine) instead of letting a missing value become a plausible wrong one.
Table-test the mapper: golden payloads, boundary cases, unknown enum values, defaults and units — mapping bugs are silent by nature.
Prefer generated or declared mapping (compile-time mappers, serializer attributes, schema validation) for large mechanical shapes, and keep hand-written code for conversions with real semantics.
Keep identity and aggregate invariants intact: rebuild through constructors or factories rather than setting fields, and keep one object per identity where the model requires it.
Batch or stream when mapping collections on hot paths instead of allocating an intermediate graph per element.
Pin the contract across the boundary — consumer-driven contract tests or golden payloads — so either representation can change without the mapping drifting.
Pair the mapper with an Identity Map when loading from a database: the same logical entity must deserialize to the same object instance, not a new copy per mapping call.
Integrate with a Unit of Work at persistence boundaries so that dirty tracking, deferred writes and conflict detection are owned by the UoW, not smuggled into the mapper.
Keep domain objects free of mapping annotations or persistence concerns: if a mapper must read through a domain object's internals to reconstruct it, the domain model has already leaked.
Version mapper output explicitly (for example a v1 and v2 mapper) so that API consumers on old shapes keep working while new ones adopt the revised representation.
When mapping to or from a third-party SDK or vendor schema, treat that schema as read-only: never let the external type's mutability cross into your mapper's output.
sources: Fowler, Patterns of Enterprise Application Architecture (2003) — Mapper (Base Patterns, ch. 18, p. 473): 'An object that sets up a communication between two independent objects'; Data Mapper (ch. 10, p. 165) is its most widely used specialization. (accessed 2026-09-20)

Fowler, Data Mapper — 'A layer of mappers that moves data between objects and a database while keeping them independent of each other and the mapper itself' (PoEAA ch. 10, p. 165). (accessed 2026-09-20)

Evans, Domain-Driven Design (2004) — introduces Anti-Corruption Layer as the pattern that isolates a domain from foreign systems; mapper is the translation engine inside that layer. (accessed 2026-09-20)

Vernon, Implementing Domain-Driven Design (2013) — discusses why the Data Mapper (as used by Hibernate, JPA, Doctrine) is preferred over Active Record in complex aggregate models. (accessed 2026-09-20)

Microsoft .NET Team, 'Domain-Driven Design with Modern .NET' — covers Data Mapper as the mechanism behind ORMs such as Entity Framework Core and Dapper, with guidance on keeping mappers idempotent and free of business logic. (accessed 2026-09-20)
MapStruct Reference Guide — its annotation processor generates type-safe bean-mapping implementations at compile time using plain getter/setter calls rather than reflection. (accessed 2026-09-21)
AutoMapper Configuration documentation — profiles and CreateMap define convention-based .NET object-to-object mappings, with configuration that can be validated before use. (accessed 2026-09-21)
SQLAlchemy 2.0 Declarative Mapping documentation — declarative mapping maps Python classes to database tables and configures their mapped properties. (accessed 2026-09-21)

Jimmy Bogard, AutoMapper Usage Guidelines — warns against using convention-based mapping for complex maps or business logic and recommends explicit alternatives when configuration becomes bespoke. (accessed 2026-09-21)
pitfalls: Letting either side hold a reference to the other side's type re-couples the subsystems and undoes the pattern.
Mapping that renames members but ignores semantics (units, time zones, absent versus default, unknown enum values) produces plausible wrong data.
A mapper that grows validation or business rules becomes a shadow domain model nobody owns.
No policy for unknown and newly added fields: one direction drops them silently and the other invents defaults.
Bidirectional sync loops: mapping A→B then B→A back into the same call stack without an identity barrier, creating infinite recursion or corrupted state.
N+1 on hot paths: lazy-loading a domain object's associations inside a mapper over a collection, triggering one additional query per element.

Mapping explosion: one mapper per pair multiplies across every new type added, leading to a boilerplate explosion that teams paper over with generic reflection-based mappers — which then silently drop or mistranslate fields.
Round-trip identity loss: loading a persisted object, passing it through a mapper, and writing it back produces a new row or version instead of an update because the identity field was not preserved.
Leaking lazy proxies or ORM proxies through the mapper boundary so callers inadvertently depend on uninitialized infrastructure rather than the domain.
Version skew between the mapper and its two representations: a field is added to the source but not to the mapper, and the target silently receives a default instead of the real value.
Using the mapper as a service layer: stacking queries, business rules or orchestration behind what looks like a simple translation, making the mapper untestable in isolation.
Ignoring the directionality of mapping: treating to_domain and to_source as mirror images when their absent/null/default policies should differ.

Wrong move: Treat a convention-based mapper as a schema contract -> renamed or semantically changed members can pass through as defaults or omissions -> instead fail on unmapped members and validate configuration or golden payloads in CI.

Wrong move: Use one bidirectional mapper for create/update commands and read models -> server-owned fields or immutable state can be overwritten -> instead define direction-specific mappers and construct changes through domain commands or factories.

Wrong move: Map a polymorphic boundary by concrete-type guesses -> subtype data can be silently flattened into the base shape -> instead encode discriminator and version handling explicitly and reject unknown variants.

related_patterns_notes.data-mapper: The most common specialization: a Data Mapper moves data between in-memory domain objects and a relational or document database, keeping both ignorant of each other. Mapper is the general pattern; Data Mapper is its ORM-specific realization.
related_patterns_notes.messaging-mapper: Another specialization where the two representations are a domain object and a message payload (command or event). The mapper holds serialization semantics including headers, content types and schema version negotiation.
related_patterns_notes.converter: A Converter handles a single value-level conversion (string→date, cents→money) and is typically a pure static function. A mapper composes many converters but also handles structural translation (field rename, shape restructure) that no single converter can express.
related_patterns_notes.adapter: An Adapter exposes a different interface to the same underlying component, bridging the API shape without changing the data itself. A mapper bridges the data representation; an adapter bridges the call interface. They compose well: an adapter may use a mapper internally.
related_patterns_notes.anti-corruption-layer: An Anti-Corruption Layer (Evans DDD) uses one or more mappers as its translation engine to keep a legacy or foreign subsystem from polluting the local domain model. The layer decides what crosses and enforces it — the mapper provides the mechanism.
related_patterns_notes.data-transfer-object: A DTO is a dumb data container that crosses a process or network boundary. Mappers commonly translate between domain objects and DTOs; the DTO has no behaviour and no knowledge of the domain, making it a clean target for the mapper.
related_patterns_notes.repository: A Repository (Fowler PoEAA ch. 13) provides a collection-like interface for accessing domain objects. It typically uses a Data Mapper internally to hydrate and persist those objects, but the Repository's contract is the domain's persistence query surface — not the mapping itself.
related_patterns_notes.unit-of-work: A Unit of Work (Fowler PoEAA ch. 11) tracks dirty objects, deferred writes and concurrency conflicts within a business transaction. It is the natural caller of a persistence-bound mapper: the UoW triggers the mapper at flush time, so mapping stays transactional and idempotent.
related_patterns_notes.identity-map: An Identity Map (Fowler PoEAA ch. 11) ensures each logical entity is loaded once and returned as the same in-memory instance. It pairs naturally with a Data Mapper at persistence boundaries to prevent round-trip amnesia and duplicate object creation.
related_patterns_notes.lazy-load: Lazy Load defers data retrieval until the property is first accessed. A mapper that touches a lazy association triggers that load, making the mapper a common source of N+1 query problems when iterating collections without eager fetching configured.
related_patterns_notes.remote-facade: A Remote Facade (Fowler PoEAA ch. 15) provides a coarse-grained operations interface over a fine-grained object graph to reduce network chattiness. It frequently uses DTOs and mappers to translate between the coarse remote shape and the fine-grained domain model.
related_patterns_notes.separated-interface: A Separated Interface (Fowler PoEAA ch. 18) defines an interface in a package that neither contains nor references the implementation. A mapper is a natural implementation of a separated interface at a persistence or integration boundary, decoupling the domain from the infrastructure package.
related_patterns_notes.assembler: An Assembler (Fowler PoEAA) is closely related to Mapper but specifically constructs a complex domain object graph from simpler input data, often involving multiple source objects. Where Mapper translates between two representations, Assembler builds a composed structure from several.
related_patterns_notes.value-object: Value Objects are immutable, identity-lacking domain components such as money or date ranges. Mappers frequently convert between a VO and its primitive or DB representation, and the immutability constraint means mapping is inherently idempotent in the VO→primitive direction.
